vignette:
Margaret, a 63-year-old European American sculptor, had spent much of her adult life working with her hands in a bright studio attached to the back of her home, shaping clay and stone into faces, bodies, and abstract forms. She had been married for many years, lived a relatively steady life, and was known among friends as private but composed. That changed after she was raped, an assault she described with visible effort and a kind of stunned precision, as though the facts remained sharper than any sense of safety around them. In the immediate aftermath, she found herself moving through the days on autopilot, aware that something in her had been permanently altered, even before she could put words to it. What stayed with her most was not only what had been done to her, but how powerless and exposed she had felt while it was happening, and how alone she felt once it was over.

In the months that followed, Margaret began to notice that certain moments could pull her back with startling force. Comments about sexual violence, even when made indirectly on the news or in ordinary conversation, could jolt her into a rigid silence. She would go still, her attention narrowing, as if the room had suddenly become dangerous. Sirens had a similar effect. When emergency vehicles passed near her home or sounded in the distance, she would tense and listen, the noise carrying her immediately into the sensation of alarm that had accompanied the assault and its aftermath. She also found that familiar people connected in some way to the event were difficult to be around. Even a name, a mention, or the possibility of encountering someone linked to that period could leave her feeling unsettled and guarded, as though proximity itself carried risk.

Over time, Margaret came to organize her life around a very small set of places that felt manageable. She said she only felt safe in a limited number of settings, and this had become a practical rule as much as an emotional one. Her home, her studio, and a few trusted routes between them were the spaces in which she could lower her guard even slightly. Everywhere else required vigilance. If she was in a shop, at an appointment, or in an unfamiliar part of town, she remained on watch for what might happen next, scanning people and exits with an intensity that made ordinary outings exhausting. She noticed, too, that sudden movement nearby could make her react as if she were in immediate danger. A person turning quickly behind her in the studio, a colleague reaching across her line of sight, or someone stepping unexpectedly into her peripheral vision could leave her flinching before she had time to think. She hated how automatic it felt, as though her body had decided before she had.

As the months became years, Margaret's understanding of herself grew increasingly harsh. She had come to believe she had acted in ways that went against who she was, and this belief carried a heavy, corrosive shame. She struggled to reconcile the assault with the image she had held of herself as capable, discerning, and principled, and in that struggle she directed blame inward with a severity she could not easily set aside. She also felt deeply let down by the people and institutions that should have protected her. That sense of institutional failure remained vivid for her, not as an abstract idea but as a personal abandonment that left her with the conviction that she had been on her own when it mattered most. Over time, she found that nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore. The work that had once given structure to her days could still be done, but it no longer held the same vitality. She continued to sculpt, yet much of the pleasure and purpose had drained away, replaced by a mechanical persistence that surprised even her.

At home, her husband noticed how carefully she chose where to sit, how easily she startled, and how often she seemed to retreat into herself after some small cue she did not want to explain. In her studio, where she had once felt most alive, she now positioned herself near the door and became uneasy when visitors or assistants moved abruptly behind her. Even the physical gestures of sculpting-lifting, turning, chiseling-could leave her taut with alertness if there was unexpected motion nearby. She had stopped attending certain community events and avoided conversations that might turn to violence or to people associated with the assault, and this narrowing of her world had slowly altered the shape of her marriage and daily life. She no longer trusted her own ease in ordinary places, and she mourned that loss with a quiet despair.

By the time she sought help, Margaret was not only distressed by the force of the reminders but frightened by how small her world had become and how empty it now felt to her. She wanted relief from the constant sense of danger and from the shame and bitterness she carried, but what brought her in most urgently was the fear that she could spend the rest of her life trapped in the same limited circuit of safe places, forever unable to feel at home in the wider world again.
